Candidate Intake

The Honorable Guild of Exterminators

Candidate Intake · Paingokgo Chapter · Eastern Tusque
Conducted by the Guild helmet. Recorded by whoever can write.

“Sit down. Not there. There.

“I am the intake. No, I am not the helmet; I am the thing inside it, which is a distinction nobody in this chapter has troubled to learn in forty years. They call me the Kettle. I would rather they did not. You may ask my name. I will not tell you today.

“Here is how this goes. Most people who come through that door cannot read, which is not a failing, it is a policy, and we will get to whose. So I ask and you answer, out loud, and this little bit of magic records the answers.

“Some of what goes on this form I will simply tell you. The sky the night you began. What was standing about. Where the mark came out. You were not consulted at the time and you are not being consulted now. The rest is what you say back to me, and there I have no opinion worth the name, so speak freely and at length. I am not going anywhere.”

What this is, out of character: a worksheet for the first session of making a player character — where you came from, what you look like, and what sort of person you are. It is not a character sheet. Nothing here records a hit point. You will still need to roll ability scores, pick a class, and buy equipment; the last page tells you how what you write here feeds into those choices. The reason we are doing all this is that this world is, quite intentionally, unwritten. We don’t know what jobs people have, how they organize societies, what the recent history of different places has been. The game is meant to have those concepts emerge organically. So, this is a way to help you think about your character while not dropping you into an archetype (farmer’s 3rd son, daughter of a noblewoman). The answers are actually MORE important here than they normally would be, but I don’t want to answer major questions about how the world works before we even sit down.

What the dice are, and what they are not. The two registers on this form are worth keeping straight.

Where you roll, the helmet is telling you something. These are facts about your character that your character never chose — the sky on a night they were not present for, an animal that happened to be in the room, where a mark came out on their skin. Nobody selects those. The dice stand in for the world having already decided.

Where you write, your character is answering. Nothing constrains those but you.

Every roll can be overruled: each one drops into a box you can type over. But roll first, look at what you got, and then decide. The point is to put a possibility in front of you that you would not have reached for, so that when you choose you are choosing against something. A character assembled entirely from preferences comes out as a list of the things you already like.

Part One · What Your Body Is

“Name first. Everybody has one and almost nobody has only one.”

The name you answer to

A use-name, if you have one — what people actually call you

A use-name is usually about your mark, your trade, or one incident you would rather was forgotten. You do not get to choose it; you only get to choose whether you answer to it. Leave it blank if nothing has stuck yet — and if there is a story behind it, save it for the table.

“Now the body. This part I do; you sit there.

“You are a composite, like everyone. Your parents gave you the frame. Whatever happened to be standing about at the hour you were begun gave you the surface. Confluence, they call it, and it is so ordinary that the only interesting question was never whether you are marked. It is by what — and what the people around you decided that was worth.”

1 Your kind

“Your parents settled the deep architecture — bone, organ, the frame the mind is hung on. Nothing that stood in that room touched any of it. Humanoid parents make a humanoid child, every time, in every province, and I have been listening to people insist otherwise since before this town had a wall.

“So. What sort of body, not what sort of people — I have no patience for the second and neither has the world, as anyone who has met two siblings in this town can tell you. Just the frame. How big, how hard to dent, how far you see once the lamp is out.”

I am

  • Aasimar — lit from within, mends by touch
  • Dragonborn — plated, with a breath that carries
  • Dwarf — dense, durable, the best dark-sight there is
  • Elf — long-limbed, sharp-sensed, barely sleeps
  • Gnome — small, quick, hard to push on
  • Goliath — very large and strong in proportion
  • Halfling — small, lucky, difficult to keep track of
  • Human — unremarkable in every direction, and quick to learn
  • Orc — heavy-built, dark-sighted, hard to put down
  • Tiefling — warm to the touch, horned or tailed or worse

We are not playing with races. Nothing in this game turns on which line you pick, nobody in the world will ask you about it, and no part of this sheet refers back to it. It is here because the rules hand out bonuses through it, and those bonuses are one of the ways the system keeps characters roughly in balance with one another. That is the entire job it does.

So these are not peoples, and they are not places. Nobody here comes from a mountain hall or a forest or a warren, nobody inherits a temperament, and there is no such thing on EART-H as behaving like your kind — Confluence scrambles the visible evidence every single generation, which is rather the point of the world. What each line describes is a body: its size, what it can take, and what it can sense. Pick the frame that fits the character already in your head and move on.

Where it sits with the next four steps: this is the deep architecture, the part your parents settled — bone, bulk, plating, how far your eyes reach in the dark. Confluence marks land on top of it. A goliath frame with fox ears is entirely ordinary; so is a halfling frame with gill-lines at the neck.

Frame What that means when you are using it
Aasimar Something under the skin gives off light and does not wash off. You mend small hurts by laying hands on them, you see where others want a lamp, and searing light and the cold that rots both find less purchase on you than they should.
Dragonborn Plated across the hide, with a breath that carries and does harm at a distance. Whatever your plating turns aside, it turns aside properly. You see in the dark.
Dwarf Built dense. You wear down slower than the frame suggests and poison does poorly in you. Your dark-sight reaches twice as far as most, and you read a floor through your feet — hollow from solid, without looking.
Elf Long-limbed and light on the ground. You do not sleep so much as set the mind down for a few hours and pick it up again. Your senses run sharp, and something in you will not be charmed.
Gnome Small and quick, with a mind that is remarkably hard to push on: magic that bends other people slides off you often enough to irritate those who make a living at it. You see in the dark.
Goliath Very large, and strong in proportion. You carry what two people carry, cover ground faster than the bulk suggests, and now and then do something that reminds a room what a body that size is actually for.
Halfling Small, and difficult to keep track of: you slip through the space a larger body takes up and put that body between you and trouble. Fear gets less grip on you than on most, and your luck is measurably better than it has any right to be.
Human Unremarkable in every direction, which is the whole of the advantage. No sense sharper than standard, no hide tougher, nothing that marks you out across a room. What you have instead is range — you pick things up faster than anybody, and you are good at more than one thing.
Orc Heavy through the shoulders, dark-sight as good as it gets, and a body that declines to notice it should have stopped. You can find a second wind on demand, and once in a while you simply do not go down when you ought to.
Tiefling Warm to the touch, always, and marked in some structural way that varies wildly from body to body — horn, tail, colouring, none of it predictable. You see in the dark, and you carry a presence people notice before you have said anything.

Almost certainly your parents do not look like you, and you do not look like your brothers or sisters. This is normal and everyone knows it is normal, which does not mean it never mattered.

Write one sentence about the first time you noticed you did not match your family.

2 The hour you began

“The sky, then. Three moons, three numbers, and every town book on EART-H records a birth as four figures rather than one.”

Roll The moon was What it did
1–2 near dark Nothing. That moon lit no beast and left you no mark.
3–4 at half A faint mark — visible close to, or in certain light, or only sometimes.
5–6 at full A deep mark — plain to a stranger at ten paces.

Io (the red)    Ganymede (the green)    Deos (the blue)

You will roll one beast in What stood by for each moon that was not dark. So you may finish this part with three marks, or two, or one, or none.

Two results send you past the next two steps.

All three at full. A threefold alignment. These happen perhaps twice in a generation and are surrounded by more superstition than any other event in ordinary life. Something passed into you that was not a marking.

All three near dark. You are unmarked — a statistical rarity, and one that different provinces treat very differently. In some you were held blessed. In others you were pitied as a vessel nobody filled.

3 Your own moon

“Different question. That was the sky on one night; this is the light you work under for the whole of your life. Everything with wit enough leans toward one of the three. The lean can be trained, and training it narrows you elsewhere — strength in one light is always paid for in another. Nobody is strong under all three. People who tell you otherwise are selling something, and I have watched three generations of this town buy it.

“Two rolls. Which light is yours, which one takes from you. Then a third for how far apart they sit, because for some of you that gap is a matter of life and death and for others it is barely worth the ink.”

d6 Moon What it is the magic of
1–2 Io, the red Transformation and change. A steep retrograde orbit, and the most changeable of the three — its light falls on a quiet valley and things in it alter suddenly
3–4 Ganymede, the green Growth, healing, and everything green and living. Its charge lingers in objects longer than the others’. It passes over the same ground about once in seven days
5–6 Deos, the blue Time, memory, and divination. The steadiest and slowest, which is why every calendar on EART-H is reckoned by it

I am strong under and diminished under

d6 The swing What that means
1 Severe At your moon’s height you are formidable; under the other you are genuinely impaired, and everyone plans around it
2 Strong Your good day and your bad day are recognisably different people
3 Marked Those who work alongside you learn your calendar within a season
4 Moderate You feel it plainly. Others notice sometimes
5 Slight You notice. Almost nobody else does
6 Limited both ways The lean is real and the effects are small at either end. You are steady, which has its own uses

How wide my swing runs

Any of these three boxes can be overwritten. If you want a particular moon, or a milder swing than the dice gave you, type it in.

A wide swing means your GM will hand you good days and bad days and expect you to plan around them. That is the intended experience of this world, and it is also the part that is not to everyone’s taste — say plainly, now, how much of it you want.

Where it happened — 1d8. Change it if you would rather it were somewhere else.

“Then the beasts. One for each moon that was not dark — the light does the carrying, so a dark moon carries nothing. Roll the same creature twice and it left two marks, and the whole street will tell you it was one animal of unusual persistence.”

“The rank column is not a rule. It is what people say, which is worse, because a rule can be argued with. It is one of the few hierarchies on this world with any grip at all, and it never grips for long: the grandchild of an eagle-marked house comes out rat-marked as readily as anybody’s. I have watched it happen to a family that had a motto about it.”

5 Where it shows

“Where it shows. One roll per mark. The marks come out in outward things — colour, texture, the voice, small structural oddities, and the way a body moves when nobody is supervising it.”

How much it shows

  • Cannot be hidden, and you gave up trying a long time ago
  • Hidden under ordinary clothes if you are careful

Now write it. Two sentences, and take your time over them — this is the single most useful thing on the sheet.

The first sentence says what a stranger sees in the first three seconds. The second sentence says what you see when you catch yourself in still water.

They should not be the same sentence.

6 The unusual cases

“This next part is not for most of you. If the sky or the ground did nothing unusual at your beginning, we skip it and you may look relieved.”

If you are unmarked. No creature reached you; you are the plain product of your parents and nothing else. What did that mean where you grew up?

  • Blessed. Set apart. Possibly made to stand somewhere at festivals
  • Pitied — a vessel nobody troubled to fill
  • Suspected. Somebody’s mother thought it had been arranged
  • Nothing at all, and that indifference was itself unusual enough to notice

Who first explained it to you, what they said, and how old you were

If all three moons were full — a threefold alignment. Something passed into you that was not a marking: not colour or shape but instinct, knowledge, appetite, or memory. Choose one.

  • A skill nobody taught you and you cannot remember acquiring:
  • A fear that is not yours, attached to something harmless
  • A fragment of borrowed memory — a place, a smell, a movement you have never made
  • A compulsion that arrives at a certain hour, or in a certain light
  • Something you can do exactly once, badly, and have never been able to explain

Tell your GM about this one before the first session. It is the only entry on this sheet with teeth in it.

If you were conceived within sight of a sacred site. Near the sites, Confluence behaves unpredictably — sometimes amplified, sometimes turned into shapes no midwife can forecast. Roll 1d6.

1–2 The mark is doubled. It shows in two places and the two do not match each other
3 You carry the beast’s opposite number: its predator, or its prey
4 The mark moves. Not often, and not far. But it is not always where it was
5 The mark is of a creature that was not there, and nobody can put a name to it
6 There is no mark. There was supposed to be one. The midwife has never stopped talking about it

7 What people say about it

“Now the part I actually care about, which is not the mark. It is what was done about it.”

Was rank taken seriously where you grew up?

  • Enormously. It set who married whom
  • By some people, in some rooms
  • It was a joke, mostly, and the joke had an edge
  • Not at all — and that was rare enough that outsiders remarked on it

Has anyone ever guessed your beast wrong? What did they guess? Did you correct them?

Name one person who is kinder to you because of your mark. Name one person who is not. You do not have to have decided yet which of the two you resent more.

Part Two · Where You Are From

“Second half. Here I stop telling and start listening, and I want you to understand why before you open your mouth.

“I have been asked these questions by four hundred candidates and I have four hundred different answers, because nobody has ever settled how people ought to live on this world. Not the Guild, not the cartographers, not the ones who write the books. What you say now goes down as it stands. So take your time, and do not give me what you think I want, because I have no idea what I want and I have had a very long while to work it out.”

Nobody has written this down yet. You are writing it now.

This is not a polite fiction to make you feel involved. The social, economic and political life of EART-H is genuinely unwritten, and so is nearly all of its history. The book this world comes out of is very confident about mountains, rainfall, rivers, roads and where the food is, and almost silent about how anybody organises themselves once they get there. That silence is deliberate, and this is where it starts getting filled in.

So what you put in this part is not backstory. It is an act of creation, and your GM will write it down and keep it. Hurray!

Yes, this does mean you could wreck the place by putting something stupid here. No pressure. In practice the fix is easy: answer as though somebody is going to have to live there, because somebody is.

Before you answer any of this: look at the map

“First find yourself on the map. I will wait. I am extremely good at waiting.”

Open the player map at https://csfowler.github.io/eart-h-book/map/ and find Paingokgo first — use the search box. It sits in the rolling hills of eastern Tusque, above a river, with a small forest called the Brake pressing on the town from the north. Everything in this part of the sheet should be somewhere you could actually have travelled from, so it is worth a few minutes with the map before you answer anything.

You almost certainly want to be from Tusque, Stockholm, Centre or Salmon. These are continents, not nations — whether EART-H has anything you could call a nation is one of the things nobody has settled, and the questions below on your community is where you get a say in it. What matters here is only that all four are ground you could have walked from. Not one of them needs a boat.

Tusque is home. Anywhere on this landmass is a walk — a long one, but a walk.

Centre shares a land border with Tusque, and its nearest edge is about eleven hundred kilometres from Paingokgo. It sits at the navel of the navigable world, with the thickest traffic and some of the largest towns on EART-H, for no better reason than that everybody must pass it. A great many people who end up somewhere else set out from there.

Stockholm also borders Tusque, and its nearest edge is nearer than Salmon’s — some fifteen hundred kilometres, with a town on it inside eighteen hundred. It is nearly the size of Tusque and holds nearly as many people. What it does not have is the inner sea: it faces the wrong water, so its shipping goes out and away rather than in toward the crowded middle, and it pays for every crossing in time. A Stockholmer in Paingokgo is not exotic. They are simply from the other side of a long, dull, entirely walkable stretch of country, and they will have opinions about how it is run.

Salmon borders Tusque too, and shares more of its speech with this part of the continent than anywhere else does — which, since speech follows the roads, is proof of a well-used way between them. It is nonetheless hard country to reach: its nearest edge is some two thousand seven hundred kilometres off, and the nearest town on it is nearly three thousand, because the ground between is empty. Close, and a long way away, which is a combination this world produces often.

Everywhere else is four thousand kilometres distant at the very least, most of it across water you would need a reason to have crossed. You may still come from there. But you will need an answer for how and why, the journey took a season or more, and you will be foreign in every room you walk into for the rest of your life — which the helmet will notice within about four words.

Name the nearest town exactly as the map spells it, so your home can be put on the map afterwards.

The place sits…

  • On a river — which on EART-H means it trades like a port even far inland
  • On a coast, set back from the water the way coastal towns always are
  • On a road, at a crossing of two ways
  • On none of those, and that was rather the point

How many people

  • Under a hundred
  • A few hundred
  • A thousand or two
  • Many thousands
  • It changed, because we moved

Connected, or self-contained?

There are two worlds on EART-H: the connected one of coasts, river-towns and sea-lanes, where a merchant knows next season’s grain price already; and the other, of mountain, deep forest and dry plain, where a community lives by its own hands and knows its neighbours and very little further. Neither is the poorer. They are different in kind.

  • Connected. Things arrived from outside constantly, and we knew where from
  • Connected badly — one road, one boat a season, and everything came through it
  • Self-contained. We made what we used
  • Self-contained on purpose. People had looked at what a market offered and declined it

Name one thing that came in from outside, and how often

9 What your community did about the moons

“Now this question is just for me. I have a running bet with a cartographer comes through every now and then about the ways that people find to screw up their lives. So, your community. Every settlement on this world is up against one problem and only one, and everything else follows from what they did about it.”

Every people on EART-H is up against the same problem: what a place yields, and what a person can do, surges and fails as the three moons wheel over it. The three keep different periods, none of them tidy and none of them in step, so the pattern over any one valley is fiercely irregular — but it is not unknown. Reading the moons is the first survival skill anybody learns. Every settlement has people who can tell you what is coming and roughly when, and the good ones are worth more than a tall stone wall any day.

What differs from place to place is not whether they know. It is what they do with knowing: what work they organise around the surges, what they put by against the failures, and who ends up holding anything when a lean stretch runs long. No hold on a piece of ground outlasts the moons’ wandering, which is why we don’t have the advent of a purely agriculture-based feudalism, and why the answer to this question is different everywhere you go.

Both questions below are about your community as a whole, not about your own household and not about what you personally did for a living. What did the settlement, taken together, organise itself around?

What my community built its living on

  • Taking the surges where they fell. We stayed put, worked flat out through a bloom, and lived very thin between
  • Following the spreaders. The settlement itself moved with it, and kept only what it could carry
  • Working the dull ground. Poor but steady, on the reasoning that a small yield you can count on beats a great one you cannot
  • Carriage and exchange. We did not grow it. We moved it, between valleys whose surges never fell at the same time
  • Keeping. Granaries, salt, ice, cellars. Our whole art was making one surge last until the next
  • The reckoning. We read the moons and sold what we knew to everyone who needed it
  • The site. Divine power sat here, and those who came to it fed us
  • A divided year. One trade while the surge lasted and an entirely different one between, and everybody did both
  • Something else:

What my community did when it went wrong

  • We moved. When the reading said to, the whole community went
  • We shared out. A bad year for one household was a bad year for everybody, by arrangement
  • We hid. Cellars, blank walls, and things one does not do in the open
  • We paid. Somebody stronger, in food or labour or children
  • We mixed. No two neighbours are strong in the same moon, and this was arranged deliberately, by someone
  • We gathered and scattered. Under one head for part of the year, dispersed into families for the rest, and both were entirely normal
  • We armed. What we had, we kept, and everyone knew it
  • We took. From the next valley over, when their surge came and ours did not
  • Something else:

Was there anyone in the community who could tell other people what to do?

  • No. The idea would have struck us as funny
  • Yes, but only while a particular stretch lasted
  • Yes, but only about certain things — namely:
  • Yes. Entirely

On what did it rest?

  • Wealth. They held the stores, or the boats, or the debts
  • Violence. They could hurt you, and had
  • Piety. They spoke for the site, or read the moons, or both
  • Descent. Their family had always done it and nobody could remember starting
  • Election. We picked them, and could unpick them
  • Competence. They were simply the best at the thing that mattered most that year
  • Knowledge. They could read, or reckon, or remember, and the rest of us could not
  • Something else:

What were they called? One word. Invent it if nothing fits — this is the word your people used, and after today it is the word EART-H uses.

And how long did it hold?

  • Their lifetime
  • Their family’s, so far, and everyone is waiting
  • About three years, and then it didn’t
  • Longer than anyone can account for, which people find unsettling
  • Something else:

10 What was held in common, and what was not

“Property. Sit forward, this is another part of my bet with that damn cartographer and I want a real answer.”

Somewhere between what belongs to everybody and what belongs to one person, every settlement draws a line. Where a people draws it says more about them than almost anything else: it is a standing answer to the question of what a person owes the rest, and what the rest owe a person.

Because the surges come and go, that line moves about far more on EART-H than it would elsewhere. Things that are common in a lean stretch are often private in a fat one, and there are places where it works the other way round.

Name something that belonged to everybody, and that anybody could use

Water, grazing, the road, the mill, the bridge, the granary, the forecast, the fishing, the woods, the shrine, the knowledge of a craft, the care of children.

Name something a person could own alone, and nobody would take

Who paid for the common things, and how?

  • Everyone gave labour, so many days a year
  • Everyone gave a share of what they took in
  • The well-off paid and were thanked for it, loudly and often
  • The well-off paid and were resented for it
  • Nobody paid; it simply held together, and outsiders found this hard to credit
  • It was falling apart, and everybody knew, and nobody would say

What happened to somebody who took more than their share?

Could one family hold the same ground two generations running?

  • Yes, and it was ordinary
  • Yes, but only the ground close to the town
  • No, and holdings were redealt — how often:
  • The question does not apply; our community did not work ground that way

11 What you were taught

“And now letters, which is where I take an interest, being a thing that talks for a living to people who were never taught to read a word of what gets written down about them. You will notice I did not say that neutrally.”

Reading, reckoning and the keeping of records are not evenly spread on EART-H. In some places every child gets them; in others they are the property of a house, an order, or one family, and are guarded accordingly. This matters more here than it would elsewhere, because so much of what keeps a settlement alive — the moon tables, the granary accounts, the words carved on the sacred sites — only works for somebody who can read it.

Where you grew up, how was knowledge handled?

  • An order kept it. It lived in a house of adepts. You got it by being taken in, and you gave them your life in exchange
  • Everyone got the beginnings. Letters and numbers to every child, free, and after that you were on your own
  • Everyone got all of it. Schooling well into adulthood, expected of everybody, and a person without it was pitied
  • It was taught to make us agree. What was taught was chosen for what it would make us believe, and we found out late
  • It was sold. Anyone who could pay; nobody who could not
  • It passed hand to hand. No schooling of any kind. You learned your work from whoever was doing it in front of you
  • It was withheld. Deliberately. Somebody had worked out what letters purchase and did not intend to share
  • Something else:

Can you read?

  • Easily
  • Slowly, and you hate doing it where people can watch
  • Only the words you were drilled on, learned by heart — which is not the same thing, and you know it
  • No

Who did you learn the most from? Name them, and say what they taught you.

Name one thing you know that few people around you know.

12 How you came to be here

“Last of it. Why you are here and not there. And yes, lots of you just make stuff up. Good for you, it’s not like we are terribly picky, so not sure why you would bother to hide it.”

1 The moons turned and your community’s answer stopped working
2 A debt. Yours, or somebody’s you could not refuse
3 You were sent. There was a purpose. You are no longer certain you are still pursuing it
4 A death changed who owned what
5 You were the one they could most easily spare
6 Somebody found out something about you
7 You left with someone. They are not with you now
8 Your mark. Somebody made your life narrow on account of it
9 Work. There was none there and there is some here
10 You wanted to see it. That is the entire reason and you are tired of apologising for it
11 You were following a road you had been told about, and it ran out here
12 You do not say. Decide the true answer privately and tell only the GM

“And why this trade, of all the trades available to a person with limbs.”

1 It pays weekly. Almost nothing pays weekly
2 They take anyone. At the time, that mattered
3 You turn out to be good at it, which surprised you more than anyone
4 Somebody local was hurt by a thing you could have handled
5 You want to be in a Guild — any Guild — for what a Guild is, not for what it does
6 The Guild goes places. You want to go places and this is a way to be fed on the road
7 A favour, a debt, or somebody’s name you dropped in the wrong room
8 You are hunting something specific and this is cover. Tell the GM what

What did you bring with you that you should have left behind?

Who do you owe? Name them, name the amount, and say whether it is money

How long have you been in Paingokgo?

  • You arrived today
  • A few weeks
  • A season
  • You grew up here, and watched the last Guild team leave for better pay in Rukgokai

13 The Reckoning

Tick one box in each pair — whichever is more true more often. Where both feel true, take the one you would act on at two in the morning. It scores itself as you go.

“In the old days people just walked up, made their mark, and started hunting > rats. But everything has to go through a ‘process’ now. I swear there are people who have less between their ears than I do and exist solely to generate > useless task for me. So that’s what this is; twenty-four pairs. Neither answer > is the clever one, so you may stop looking for it, and they are not > grouped in any order you can use, because I am not new at this. I have sat on this table since before your grandmother was a rumour and I have heard every flattering answer there is. Pick the true one and we will both be finished sooner.”

  1. A  Give me one room with a door that is mine and you may keep the horse. B  Give me the horse.
  2. A  What I know is worth something precisely because you do not know it. B  What I know is worth nothing until somebody else has it too.
  3. A  You cannot resign from your family. People try. It does not take. B  You can resign from your family, and some people should have done it years ago.
  4. A  What a person shows you is mostly what they are. B  What a person shows you is the part they picked out that morning.
  5. A  Teach it badly to ten people rather than well to one. B  Teach it well to one. The other nine may watch.
  6. A  First thing I do in a new building is find the way out of it. B  First thing I do in a new building is find out who keeps it.

“Six down. You are doing fine. That is not praise, it is arithmetic.”

  1. A  The question I want answered is the one nobody has asked yet. B  The question I want answered is the obvious one, and nine times in ten it is also the answer.
  2. A  The people I would die for, I met. B  The people I would die for, I was handed at birth and never got a say.
  3. A  Things get better when you go where they are already better. B  Things get better when you stay long enough to make them better.
  4. A  I take people at their word. I also keep watching. B  I take people at their word until they hand me a reason not to.
  5. A  In trouble, I go home. B  In trouble, I go to whoever I trust, and I do not much care what map they are on.
  6. A  I lay the whole plan out and let everybody find the holes in it. B  I do not tell anybody the whole plan. Not from malice. From habit.

“Halfway. You hesitated on that last one. I noticed. I notice everything, it is the only entertainment available to me.”

  1. A  When something goes well I enjoy it. B  When something goes well I want to know exactly why, in case it does not next time.
  2. A  A crew that works beats a bloodline that does not. B  A bloodline that does not work is still a bloodline. That is rather the point of one.
  3. A  If I found a way to make the work easier I would keep it to myself a season, just to see. B  If I found a way to make the work easier I would tell the others that week.
  4. A  I have left somewhere too early, and I still turn it over. B  I have never once regretted leaving early. Not once. Ask me again in ten years.
  5. A  Generosity comes back around. It always has. B  Generosity is a thing you can run out of. I have watched it happen.
  6. A  I owe the people I came from whether or not they earned it. B  Nobody is owed anything they did not earn, and that includes the people who fed me.

“Eighteen. Nearly rid of me. Try not to look so relieved, it is unbecoming in a candidate.”

  1. A  Somebody who has moved four times has lost four times. B  Somebody who has moved four times can manage a fifth before breakfast.
  2. A  If it looks like a rat problem, it is a rat problem. B  If it looks like a rat problem, something drove the rats.
  3. A  I have built a family out of strangers before. I could do it again by winter. B  I have one family. The notion of assembling another is faintly horrifying.
  4. A  If a job can only be done by me, that is precisely why I am still employed. B  If a job can only be done by me, I have arranged something badly.
  5. A  If this town turned on me I would be gone by dark and cheerful by market day. B  If this town turned on me it would take something out of me I would not get back.
  6. A  I have been badly wrong about somebody, and I have not stopped turning it over. B  I have been badly wrong about somebody, and I got on with my day.

“Done. Hold still. I am deciding what you are, and I would rather not have to do it twice.”

Your Reckoning

My Reckoning

A three-three tie means you are genuinely on the fence. Take the letter you would rather be, and mark the tie — a person who could go either way under pressure is more playable than one who could not.

RKBP The Wall Builds a thing, holds it, and knows exactly who is inside it.Recruiter’s margin: “Give her the standing contract. Do not move her.”
RKBD The Cellar Keeps a house, keeps their own, and keeps a great deal back.“Knows more than he says. Ask twice.”
RKCP The Forge Made a household out of people they picked, and will not be shifted off it.“Loyal to the crew. Not, as yet, to us.”
RKCD The Lock Devoted to a chosen few on terms nobody outside can read.“Useful. Opaque. Find out who holds the debt.”
RGBP The Hearth Stays put and feeds whoever turns up, beginning with their own.“Everybody likes her. That is the asset, not a bonus.”
RGBD The Well Gives freely, from one place, and notes carefully who drinks.“Generous and counting. Both are true.”
RGCP The Bell Plants themselves somewhere and starts calling people to it.“Will have a following within a year. Decide now whether that suits us.”
RGCD The Threshold Holds a door open for people not born to it, and studies each one on the way through.“Recruiter material. In about ten years.”
VKBP The Pack Travels, brings their own along, and does not share the road.“Hire the whole family or none of it.”
VKBD The Cache Moves constantly and leaves things buried behind them.“Has a plan we are not in. Not necessarily one against us.”
VKCP The Company A crew, not a family. The crew’s business stays the crew’s.“Straightforward. Expensive. Worth it.”
VKCD The Shadow Goes light, chooses their people slowly, tells them less than anyone.“Excellent in the field. Do not put him in a town meeting.”
VGBP The Post Carries news, goods and people between the places their own folk are.“Half our intelligence will come through her. Pay her properly.”
VGBD The Cartographer Walks in order to be corrected, and comes back with more than they took.“Will question the charter within the month. This is not a complaint.”
VGCP The Road Belongs to whoever is walking it today, and says so out loud.“No enemies yet. Give it time.”
VGCD The Ford Turns up where two peoples meet, gives away what they know, and is nobody’s.“Trusted everywhere. Owned nowhere. Rare, and I would not waste it.”

The Four Questions

You will be asked these aloud, and you will answer aloud. GM will write it down, these are just your notes to get in character.

“Four things. Then you can go and I can be put back on the shelf.”

“What brings you to pest control?”

“The moons shifted yesterday. Io’s descending. What does that mean for a hunt?”

“You are up against something that shrugs off the best thing you can do. What then?”

“Guild members share bounties equally. Problem?”

“Fine. That is the four. NEXT!!!!!”

The Handoff

This sheet covers the half of character creation your rulebook does not. Here is how the two fit together.

What this form asked What the rules call it What you still owe
Step 1 — your kind Species Pick it and take its traits. Nothing else on the sheet refers back to it
Part Two — the life you led before Background Pick the one that fits what you wrote. It gives you three ability-score increases, two skills, one tool, and an Origin Feat
Steps 2, 4–7 — your marks Nothing mechanical Ask the GM whether a deep mark ought to do something small
Step 13 — your Reckoning Nothing. It is roleplay But it should make one Background obviously correct and two obviously wrong
Step 3 — your moon Lunar affinity, per the table rules Tell the GM the strong moon, the weak one, and how wide the swing runs
— Class Choose. Nothing on this sheet constrains it
— Ability scores Roll 4d6, drop the lowest, six times

“That is the lot. Here is the parchment with your answers for HR. Leave that on the table, put me back on the shelf face out — face out, I am not asking twice — and go and be somebody’s problem.”
